title: Design peer-to-peer backlog: a follower fills a gap from another follower, not the hub
description:
Promoted from a parked idea to a real design item by Mark, 2026-11-22
(docs/design/mimi-catchup.md §7, which was written as "not proposed,
recorded because it is the first thing anyone will ask").

THE IDEA. A follower missing sequences 400-450 asks a PEER follower that
already holds them, instead of the hub.

WHY IT IS WORTH DESIGNING, and the argument that promoted it: it spreads
read load off the hub, and it keeps working when the hub is down. The
second is a real resilience property, not an optimisation. A hub outage
stops the room accepting NEW messages, because the hub is the only
writer and its identity is in the roomId -- but READING backlog does not
need the hub at all if someone else holds the bytes. Today a hub outage
takes both.

It depends on follower catch-up existing first (mimid-1wgh.37.104): the
sequence is what makes "who holds 400 to 450" a question that can be
asked at all.

THIS IS ALSO WHERE A VECTOR CLOCK EARNS ITS PLACE. The catch-up design
concluded MIMI wants a scalar sequence, not a vector clock, because a
room has one writer (§3). That conclusion holds for the room's order and
is not reopened here. But once several followers hold overlapping
PIECES of one hub-ordered stream, "who has what" is genuinely a
per-origin holdings question, and a vector clock or an interval set is
the right shape for it. The hub's sequence stays the single authority on
ORDER; the clock describes AVAILABILITY.

OPEN DESIGN QUESTIONS, in the order they block each other:

1. Policy, and it gates everything else: may a follower serve a room's
   fanout to another follower at all? That is a question about who may
   hold and redistribute a room's history, not a transport question. It
   plausibly wants a say from the room's policy (room-policy-04) or a
   hub-published permission, because "my provider may hand my room's
   history to a provider of its choosing" is a thing a room might
   refuse.

2. Authenticity, and the piece the current design does NOT have. A
   receiver taking bytes from a peer rather than the hub needs to verify
   both the message AND its position. Franking covers hub acceptance
   where it applies, but nothing today binds a sequence to a message in
   a way a third party can check, so a relaying peer could renumber or
   omit. The natural fix is for the hub to sign a running hash over the
   fanout stream -- a hash chain, each entry over (previous, sequence,
   message digest) -- so any holder can prove a message's position and a
   gap cannot be hidden. That is a real addition to the catch-up design
   and would want to be in protocol-08 text alongside it, because
   retrofitting verifiability later is much harder than designing it in.
   Consider whether mimid-1wgh.37.104.1 should assign the chain entry at
   the same time as the sequence, even before peer-to-peer exists.

3. Discovery: how does a follower learn which peers hold 400-450, and
   does it learn that from the hub, from a peer, or by asking around?
   (See the vector clock note above.)

4. Privacy: asking a peer reveals your gap to a third party, where
   asking the hub reveals it only to a party that already knew it fanned
   out to you (§9). That is a genuine widening and must be stated.

5. Abuse: a peer that serves backlog can be used to amplify, and a peer
   that asks can probe which rooms another provider follows. Needs rate
   limits and a reason to refuse.

NOT STARTED. No text, no implementation, no WG proposal. Blocked on
mimid-1wgh.37.104 landing, and on question 1, which is Mark's or the
WG's to answer and not an implementation detail.
